title: Valuing a stream of payments
objectives: Discount a future payment to its value today
Price a fixed stream of payments as a geometric series
Value a stream that never ends

screens.prose: A bond pays £100.00 in one year. Money today can earn 5% a year, so £1.00 today grows to £1.05.
screens.question: What is that £100.00 worth today?

hints.text: Which amount today would grow to £100.00 in a year?
Growing multiplies by 1.05, so go back by dividing.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the amount that becomes £100.00 after growing by 5%.

byKey.minus: You took 5% off £100.00. But £95.00 grows to only £99.75. Divide by 1.05 instead.
byKey.grow: You grew the £100.00 for a year. We want to go back to today, so divide.
byKey.same: £100.00 today would grow to £105.00. Money later is worth less than money now.

explain.text: Today's value $V$ must grow to £100.00, so $1.05V = 100$ and $V = \text{£}95.24$. Going back in time divides by $1.05$. This is called **discounting**.

screens.prose: Now £100.00 arrives at the end of each of the next 5 years. Each dot is one payment's value today. Slide the rate.
screens.question: As the rate rises, which payment loses the most of its value today?

options.why: The year 1 payment is divided by $1 + r$ just once. The year 5 payment is divided five times.
Each payment is £100.00, but they are discounted different numbers of times.

hints.text: Slide from 0% to 20% and watch the first and last dots.
At 20% year 1 is worth £83.33 and year 5 only £40.19.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare how far the first and last dots move.

explain.text: Year $t$'s payment is worth $\tfrac{100}{(1 + r)^t}$ today. A higher rate shrinks every dot, and the later ones most, since their divisor has a higher power. At 5% the five are worth £432.95 together.

screens.prose: A payment's value today is its **present value**. At 5%, the five payments together are worth $$\frac{100}{1.05} + \frac{100}{1.05^2} + \dots + \frac{100}{1.05^5}$$
screens.question: This is a geometric series. What is its common ratio?

options.why: You used the growth factor. Each later payment is worth less, so the terms shrink.
0.05 is the rate. The ratio is what turns one term into the next.
You took 5% off each time. Dividing by 1.05 multiplies by about 0.952, not 0.95.

hints.text: How do you get from $\tfrac{100}{1.05}$ to $\tfrac{100}{1.05^2}$?
Read two neighbouring dots: £95.24, then £90.70.
Each term is the one before divided by 1.05, which is multiplying by $\tfrac{1}{1.05}$.

feedback.correct: Each term is the last one divided by 1.05.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find what each term is multiplied by to give the next.

explain.text: Each payment is a year later than the one before, so it is divided by 1.05 once more. The ratio is $\tfrac{1}{1.05} \approx 0.952$. So we can add the stream with the geometric series formula.

screens.prose: Add the five present values with $S = a\dfrac{1 - q^n}{1 - q}$, where $a = \tfrac{100}{1.05}$, $q = \tfrac{1}{1.05}$ and $n = 5$.
screens.question: What are the five payments worth today?

hints.text: Work out $q^5 = 1.05^{-5}$ first.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Put $a$, $q$ and $n$ into the formula, or add the five dots.

byKey.none: That is $5 \times \text{£}100.00$ with no discounting. Each payment is worth less today.
byKey.once: You divided all £500.00 by 1.05 once. Later payments are divided more times.
byKey.last: You discounted all £500.00 by five years. Only the last payment waits that long.

explain.text: The 1.05s cancel: $S = \tfrac{100}{0.05}(1 - 1.05^{-5}) = 2000 \times 0.216474 = \text{£}432.95$. That matches adding the dots. Waiting costs the stream £67.05 against £500.00 paid now.

screens.prose: The same £100.00 a year at 5%, but for 10 years instead of 5.
screens.question: What is the ten-year stream worth today?

options.why: You doubled the five-year value. Payments 6 to 10 come later, so each is worth less.
That is ten payments with no discounting.
You discounted all £1,000.00 by ten years. Only the last payment waits that long.

hints.text: Use the formula with $n = 10$.

explain.text: $\tfrac{100}{0.05}(1 - 1.05^{-10}) = \text{£}772.17$. Payments 6 to 10 are the first five pushed back five years. So they are worth only $1.05^{-5} \approx 0.78$ times as much.

screens.prose: Now the payments never stop: £100.00 a year for ever, at 5%. The series is infinite, but its terms shrink by the ratio $\tfrac{1}{1.05}$.

state.caption: Each payment is worth less than the one before, for ever

screens.question: What is the never-ending stream worth today?

widget.label: Value today of payments for ever

hints.text: Use the infinite sum $\tfrac{a}{1 - q}$ from adding forever.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use $\tfrac{a}{1 - q}$ with $a = \tfrac{100}{1.05}$ and $q = \tfrac{1}{1.05}$.

byKey.due: You counted a payment today as well. The first one is a year away.
byKey.pct: You divided by 5, not 0.05. In the maths, 5% is 0.05.
byKey.five: That is five years of payments. This stream never stops.

explain.text: $\tfrac{a}{1 - q} = \tfrac{100/1.05}{0.05/1.05} = \tfrac{100}{0.05} = \text{£}2{,}000.00$. Infinitely many payments have a finite value, because $1.05^{-n}$ shrinks to 0. It is the limit of $\tfrac{100}{0.05}(1 - 1.05^{-n})$ as $n$ grows.

screens.question: What are the five payments worth today?

The first payment counts in full. The other four are a year, two, three and four years away.
£100.00 plus four end-of-year payments: $100 + \tfrac{100}{0.05}(1 - 1.05^{-4})$.

feedback.correct: £100.00 now plus £354.60 for the other four.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check when each payment is made before you discount it.

byKey.formula: You used the formula from the earlier screens. It assumes the first payment comes in a year. Here it comes today, so it is not discounted.

explain.text: The first £100.00 is paid today, so it counts in full. The other four are worth $\tfrac{100}{0.05}(1 - 1.05^{-4}) = \text{£}354.60$. In all £454.60, which is $1.05 \times \text{£}432.95$: every payment is a year earlier.

screens.prose: Derive the formula for $n$ payments of $C$ at rate $r$, the first in a year. Use the shifted copy, as for any geometric series.
screens.question: Put the lines in order.

lines.text: $S = \dfrac{C}{1+r} + \dfrac{C}{(1+r)^2} + \dots + \dfrac{C}{(1+r)^n}$, the present value of each payment
$(1 + r)S = C + \dfrac{C}{1+r} + \dots + \dfrac{C}{(1+r)^{n-1}}$, multiply every term by $1 + r$
$(1 + r)S - S = C - \dfrac{C}{(1+r)^n}$, subtract: the shared terms cancel
$S = \dfrac{C}{r}\left(1 - (1 + r)^{-n}\right)$, the left side is $rS$, so divide by $r$

hints.text: Which line writes out the stream term by term?
The shifted copy must exist before anything is subtracted.
Write $S$, multiply by $1 + r$, subtract, then divide by $r$.

feedback.correct: The shifted copy cancels all but two terms.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write the sum, shift it, subtract, then solve for $S$.

byKey.subtract: Subtracting needs both $S$ and the shifted copy written first.
byKey.solve: Dividing by $r$ is the last step, once only $rS$ is left.

explain.text: Multiplying by $1 + r$ shifts every payment a year earlier. Subtracting leaves only the first and last terms: $rS = C - C(1 + r)^{-n}$. So $S = \tfrac{C}{r}(1 - (1 + r)^{-n})$, and as $n$ grows it tends to $\tfrac{C}{r}$.

screens.prose: A 3-year bond pays a £5.00 coupon at the end of each year and £100.00 back at the end. The market yield is 4% a year.

state.caption: Coupons of £5.00, then £100.00 back with the last one

screens.question: What is the bond worth today?

hints.text: Split the cash into a stream of three £5.00 coupons and one £100.00 at year 3.
The coupons are worth $\tfrac{5}{0.04}(1 - 1.04^{-3})$.
Coupons £13.88, and $\tfrac{100}{1.04^3} = \text{£}88.90$. Add them.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Discount the coupons as a stream and the £100.00 as one payment in year 3.

byKey.none: That adds the cash with no discounting. Each payment is worth less today.
byKey.coupons: That is the coupons alone. Add the £100.00 repaid in year 3, discounted.
byKey.face: That is the £100.00 repayment alone. Add the three coupons.
byKey.end: You discounted every payment by three years. The first two coupons come sooner.

explain.text: Coupons: $\tfrac{5}{0.04}(1 - 1.04^{-3}) = \text{£}13.88$. The £100.00: $\tfrac{100}{1.04^3} = \text{£}88.90$. The price, £102.78, is above £100.00 because the 5% coupon beats the 4% yield.

ideas: A payment $t$ years away is worth $\tfrac{C}{(1 + r)^t}$ today.
Equal payments form a geometric series with ratio $\tfrac{1}{1 + r}$, so the shifted copy sums them.
A stream that never ends has a finite value, $\tfrac{C}{r}$, because the terms shrink to 0.

formula.note: For $n$ payments of $C$, the first one year from today.

quiz.prose: £200.00 will be paid in 2 years. The rate is 4% a year.
quiz.question: What is it worth today?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide by 1.04 once for each year.

byKey.simple: You took 8% off. Discounting divides by $1.04^2 = 1.0816$.
byKey.once: You discounted for one year. The payment is two years away.
byKey.grow: You grew the £200.00 for two years. We want its value today, so divide.

explain.text: Two years away means dividing by 1.04 twice: $\tfrac{200}{1.04^2} = \tfrac{200}{1.0816} = \text{£}184.91$.

quiz.prose: A stream pays £50.00 at the end of every year, for ever. The rate is 2.5% a year.
quiz.question: What is it worth today?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. A stream for ever is worth $\tfrac{C}{r}$.

byKey.times: You multiplied by the rate. Divide by it.
byKey.pct: You divided by 2.5. In the maths, 2.5% is 0.025.
byKey.due: You added a payment today. The first payment is a year away.

explain.text: The infinite series sums to $\tfrac{C}{r} = \tfrac{50}{0.025} = \text{£}2{,}000.00$. A lower rate makes far-off payments worth more, so the value is large.

quiz.prose: Five payments of £100.00, one at the end of each year, are worth £432.95 at 5%.
quiz.question: The rate rises to 6%. What are they worth now?

options.why: You expected a higher rate to raise the value. A higher rate discounts each payment more.
The payments are the same, but each is now divided by 1.06, not 1.05.
You discounted all £500.00 by five years at 6%. Only the last payment waits that long.

feedback.correct: £421.24: a higher rate lowers the value.

explain.text: $\tfrac{100}{0.06}(1 - 1.06^{-5}) = \text{£}421.24$. A higher rate discounts every payment more, so the stream is worth less. That is why bond prices fall when yields rise.
